indexing.note: tracks the federal standard deduction (IRC 63, indexed under 63(c)(4)): credit base 6% of it, exemption test equal to it (59-10-1018(2)(a), 59-10-104.1(2))
CPI (IRC 1(f)(4)-(5)) vs calendar 2020; nearest dollar, joint twice single (59-10-1018(4)-(5))

not_modelled.what: The Utah personal exemption in the taxpayer tax credit: 2,111 for each dependent allowed a federal credit under IRC section 24, a dependent born in the year counted twice. It adds 6% of 2,111 to the credit for each.
Military Survivor Benefits Credit (AA): 4.5% of survivor benefits when the member died on active duty or in training. A survivor of a retired member takes AJ, which is modelled.

Previously-taxed retirement income (code 90): a section 401(a) plan distribution whose contribution was left out of federal AGI and taxed by another state. The booklet says most filers do not qualify.
Interest and dividends on U.S. Government obligations are subtracted (code 71), not FNMA or GNMA.
Utah municipal interest that is in federal AGI, such as Build America Bonds, is subtracted (code 71).
Capital Gain Transactions Credit (04) and Gold and Silver Coin Sale Credit (26): 4.5% of those gains; a projection does not hold the transactions.
Child tax credit (AT) and other credits tied to dependents, not in the record.
Credit for income tax paid to another state (17), earned income credit (AM) and other credits unrelated to retirement income, not in the record.
Part-year and nonresident returns (TC-40B), which apportion the tax and some credits.

approximations.what: Utah has no deduction from income, so base.deductions is empty on purpose. The taxpayer tax credit stands in for it: 6% of the capped income, cap = the federal standard deduction for the status, so the credit is 945 single, 1,417.50 head of household, 1,890 joint or qualifying surviving spouse, once income reaches the cap. Below the cap the credit is smaller than the form's, but 6% of income exceeds 4.5% tax either way, so tax is 0 on both. The phase-out (line 19) comes off the credit, after the 6%, as it does after the 4.5% on the Social Security credit. The cap leaves out the federal age 65 and blindness extras, which line 12 includes because it takes federal line 12e; the Utah sources print no amount for them.
approximations.size: Exact for a filer under 65 on the standard deduction with no dependents: same tax to the cent at 8 incomes per status. Above that: 6% of the extras. Using the 2025 federal extras in docs/checks-brief.md, not in Utah's sources: 120 a year single or head of household 65 or older, 96 a person married, 192 for a couple both 65 or older. It applies while any credit remains: to Utah taxable income of about 90,905 single, 136,358 head of household, 181,811 joint, plus up to 9,231 or 7,385 a person for the extras. So nearly every retired household in those ranges sees this error.

approximations.what: The credit uses the standard deduction for everyone. A federal itemizer's line 12 is the itemized total and line 14 takes out state and local income tax, so the credit base is itemized deductions less that tax. A separate filer whose spouse itemized has a standard deduction of 0.
approximations.size: 6% of the difference, while the credit lasts: a joint itemizer with 45,000 itemized including 6,000 of state income tax has a base of 39,000 against 31,500, so 450 a year overstated tax.

approximations.what: The Qualified Exempt Taxpayer threshold is the standard deduction only. The worksheet adds the federal enhanced deduction for seniors (Schedule 1-A line 37), which the Utah sources print no amount for and the format can't hold.
approximations.size: Only for federal AGI between the threshold and the threshold plus line 37, where the true tax is 0. With an illustrative line 37 of 6,000 a person, the projection's tax is at most 79.73 single at AGI 21,750 and 159.46 joint at 43,500. This overlaps the age extras error above; the two do not add.

approximations.what: The Social Security credit's measure maps to federal AGI plus tax-exempt interest. The worksheet takes line 9, removes the code 57 addition and adds all tax-exempt interest. That is the mapped measure less lines 7 and 8, so it leaves subtractions in: U.S. obligation interest, railroad retirement, a state tax refund. State taxable income plus tax-exempt interest was rejected: it counts added-back municipal interest twice.
approximations.size: 2.5% of those subtractions, only while the credit is being phased out: 20,000 of Treasury interest costs up to 500 a year, limited to the credit itself.

approximations.what: The Retirement Credit and Social Security credit's measures, and the state income, leave out the rarer additions and the line 7 refund: lump sum distribution (51), MSA and my529 addbacks, trust income, equitable adjustments.
approximations.size: 4.5% of the amount in tax. Rare for a planning household.

approximations.what: The Retirement Credit's worksheet takes one reduction on the return, from 450 or 900. The relief is per person, so a consumer that takes the whole reduction from each person's 450 reduces a couple's credit twice.
approximations.size: Only for a couple both born by 1952-12-31 with modified AGI over 32,000. Largest at 50,000: 450 by the worksheet, 0 if reduced twice. A consumer that reduces the 900 once has no error.

approximations.what: The Retirement Credit is barred with both AH and AJ, for either spouse on a joint return, but AH and AJ can be taken together. The true choice is 18 against AH plus AJ together. cannot_combine_with is pairwise and can't state that, so a consumer comparing 18 with each one alone may keep 18 when the two together are better. No best_of_group is used: it would stop AH with AJ, and it is evaluated per person while this bar is on the return.
approximations.size: Only for someone born by 1952-12-31 with both Social Security and military retirement, when each credit alone is below 18 and their sum is above it. Under 450 a year single, under 900 joint.

approximations.what: U.S. obligation interest is taxed (not_modelled): the projection cannot tell it from other interest.
approximations.size: 4.5% of the interest, more inside the credit phase-outs: 10,000 of Treasury interest, 450 a year, or 580 inside the taxpayer tax credit phase-out.

approximations.what: All other-state municipal interest is added back. The booklet adds it only for bonds acquired after Jan. 1, 2003, and not when the issuer does not tax bonds issued by Utah or the issuing state has no income tax, so it depends on the issuing state. A projection that cannot tell Utah bonds from others treats all as other-state.
approximations.size: 4.5% of the interest wrongly added, more inside the credit phase-outs: 10,000 of Texas or Florida bond interest, 450 a year.

approximations.what: Brackets, the credit's cap and base amounts, and the credit thresholds are held flat (the booklet does not say they are indexed). The cap is the federal standard deduction, which line 12 takes from each year's federal return, so holding it flat is the larger effect.
approximations.size: Grows with the years: each 1% the federal deduction rises is worth 9.45 of credit single, 18.90 joint. Rate cuts such as 2025's are not carried forward either.
